final_proof:
Work in ZF, without invoking the Axiom of Choice. We use the standard fact, provable in ZF by transfinite recursion, that every well-ordered set is order-isomorphic to a unique ordinal (its order type).

Let \(W\) be the set of all pairs \((B,R)\) such that \(B\subseteq\omega\) and \(R\subseteq B\times B\) well-orders \(B\). This is a set because it is a definable subset of \(\mathcal P(\omega)\times\mathcal P(\omega\times\omega)\). By Replacement, the collection
\[
\Omega=\{\operatorname{otp}(B,R):(B,R)\in W\}
\]
is a set of ordinals.

An ordinal \(\alpha\) belongs to \(\Omega\) exactly when there is an injection from \(\alpha\) into \(\omega\). Indeed, if \(\alpha=\operatorname{otp}(B,R)\) for a well-ordered \(B\subseteq\omega\), the order isomorphism \(\alpha\to B\), followed by the inclusion \(B\hookrightarrow\omega\), is such an injection. Conversely, if \(f:\alpha\to\omega\) is injective, put \(B=f[\alpha]\) and transport the ordinal order on \(\alpha\) to \(B\): declare \(f(\xi)R f(\eta)\) if and only if \(\xi<\eta\). Then \((B,R)\in W\) and has order type \(\alpha\), so \(\alpha\in\Omega\).

It follows that \(\Omega\) is transitive. For if \(\alpha\in\Omega\) and \(\beta\in\alpha\), then \(\beta\subseteq\alpha\), so restricting an injection \(\alpha\to\omega\) gives an injection \(\beta\to\omega\), whence \(\beta\in\Omega\). A transitive set all of whose members are ordinals is itself an ordinal; hence \(\Omega\), ordered by \(\in\), is a well-ordered set.

There is no injection \(\Omega\to\omega\). If there were one, the characterization just proved, applied to the ordinal \(\Omega\), would imply \(\Omega\in\Omega\), which is impossible for an ordinal because membership is irreflexive on ordinals. Thus \(\Omega\) is uncountable.

Finally, every proper initial segment of the ordinal \(\Omega\) has the form
\[
\{\beta\in\Omega:\beta<\alpha\}=\alpha
\]
for some \(\alpha<\Omega\). Since \(\alpha<\Omega\) means \(\alpha\in\Omega\), the characterization of \(\Omega\) supplies an injection \(\alpha\to\omega\); hence that initial segment is countable.

Here “countable” may be read as “injects into \(\omega\).” If instead it is defined as “finite or in bijection with \(\omega\),” these formulations agree in ZF: an infinite subset of \(\omega\) can be enumerated in increasing order, so no choice principle is required. Therefore, in ZF alone, \(\Omega\) is an uncountable well-ordered set all of whose proper initial segments are countable.
